text: Every pattern in this chapter so far was framed around reliability and latency. Each one is also, directly, a cost decision -- because GPU instances are priced meaningfully higher per hour than typical CPU instances.

Rereading this chapter's levers through a cost lens: max instances is the hard ceiling on worst-case cost, every cache hit is an inference call you don't pay for, and a queue absorbs a burst with existing capacity instead of immediately paying for new instances.

Spot or preemptible instances are sixty to ninety percent cheaper than on-demand, but can be reclaimed by the cloud provider with little warning. They're a great fit for batch jobs and queue-and-worker patterns, a bad fit when a user is actively waiting on that exact request.

Traffic and latency alerts answer whether the service is healthy. A cost alert answers a different question: is it still cheap enough to run this way? A service can be perfectly healthy and still be quietly burning far more than expected.
That closes out scaling and reliability. Everything from here is the capstone -- taking a real AI app through containerizing, deploying, and autoscaling it end to end.
